No other language that uses the same letters as %1$s has a layout to offer.
Not downloaded. Each key types the character printed on it.
Download failed. Press to try again.

resources.string: These come from the Keyman project, an open collection of keyboards for languages that rarely get one. Many of them decide what a key types from rules rather than from the character printed on it, and those download a few kilobytes from keyman.com the first time you switch one on.
None of these layouts is on. Tap a card to turn one on.
Try again to download typing rules for %1$s
Until you download them again, each key of this layout types the character printed on it.
Delete a whole cluster like %1$s as one unit

Backspace usually deletes one code point at a time. This sometimes leaves half-formed clusters on the screen. With this setting on, one press deletes the whole cluster while you type %1$s. Other languages keep their own setting.
Fix typos when you press space

Turn this off to keep each word you type in %1$s as you typed it, while other languages are still corrected. The suggestion strip still shows its suggestions, and you can tap one. The autocorrect switch in Typing turns autocorrect off for all languages.
Add a space when you select a word from the suggestion strip

Turn this off to type a word you select from the suggestion strip in %1$s without a space after it, so you can add an ending straight away. Other languages still get the space. The Space after a suggestion switch in Typing turns the space off for all languages.
Type "tmr" to get তোমার, and "table" to get টেবিল

Some words are not spelled the way they sound. "Table" is written টেবিল, not তাবলে, and people type "tmr" for তোমার with no vowels at all. This setting uses a list of those spellings while you type %1$s, so you get the word people write. Turn it off to get the letter-for-letter reading instead. Other languages keep their own setting.
Type "asi" to get আছি instead of আসি

Romanized typing is loose, so when you press space the keyboard can replace what you typed with a dictionary word that sounds the same. "asi" becomes আছি, the word people usually mean. This happens even with autocorrect off, because it is part of how %1$s is typed. Turn it off to always get exactly what the typing rules spell. The dictionary words still show in the suggestion strip, so you can tap one. Known spellings have their own setting above.
Pick the reading that fits the words you already typed

One romanized spelling can stand for several %1$s words. With this on, the keyboard looks at the one or two words you typed just before and moves up the reading that usually follows them, both in the suggestion strip and for what the space bar writes. It learns from what you type, and from the downloaded word-pair data where your language has it. A known spelling only trades places with another known spelling of the same word, so what you see while typing is still what space writes. Turn this off if the keyboard picks a different word than you expect after certain words.
Show the letter each key types
Put the %1$s a key is about to write in its corner

A phonetic layout types %1$s from roman keys, so the keys do not show what they write. This puts the answer in the corner of each key, and it follows the word you are typing: a k is ক at the start of a word, but after a consonant the same key joins to it. Shift changes the hints too, because a phonetic layout reads capitals as different letters. Choose how much of the joined letter to show. "Added" shows only the part the key writes. "Whole letter" repeats the consonant before it, so the hint is a shape that appears in real words.
The keys show only their roman letter
The corner shows only the part that the key writes
The corner repeats the consonant before it, so the hint is a shape from a real word
Vowels, consonants, signs and the full guide
The first letter is the vowel on its own. The second is the sign it becomes after a consonant.

Two consonants in a row join into one letter where Bangla has that letter: "kt" is ক্ত, but "kb" stays কব. An r, y or w after a consonant always joins as a fola, and reph is a double r. Type a vowel between two consonants to keep them apart.
Whether two consonants join is a guess from how the word is said. The suggestion strip offers the other reading.
Between two consonants, keeps them apart
At the start of a word
Every rule with examples, on the WM Keyboard website
The lettering the fancy keyboard types. Also switchable from the strip over the keys.

Make a style from any alphabet: copy a font\'s letters from a fancy-text website and paste them in. Your fonts join the strip over the keys after the built-in styles. Letters you leave out type plain. Separate the letters with spaces to give one letter several characters, such as (a) (b) (c).
Paste an alphabet and type in it from the strip
Room for 50 fonts. Delete one to add another.
No fonts of your own yet.
%1$d of 26. Paste a to z, or a to z, A to Z and 0 to 9 in one go.
%1$d of 26. Left empty, capitals type the small letters.
%1$d of 10. Left empty, digits stay plain.
%1$d characters, more than %2$d. Separate letters with spaces if one letter is several characters.
For upside-down letters: the line is reversed so it reads with the phone turned round. Types letter by letter, without suggestions.
A tone key is a letter unless the word is one the language spells

Telex and VNI mark a tone whenever the vowels allow it, so typing fas gives fá even though f is not a Vietnamese onset and there is no word there. With this on, a tone key that would land on something that is not a word is typed as the letter it is drawn as instead, and only a syllable the language actually spells takes a tone. mix is still mĩ, because that is a word.
With the Vietnamese word list, tieng becomes tiếng when it can only be one word

Telex and VNI type only the marks you spell. With this on, a word you finish without one of its marks gets it from the Vietnamese word list, but only when the list has one way to read it: tieng becomes tiếng and duong becomes đường. A word the list already has is never changed, and a spelling like toan, which can be toàn, toán or toản, stays as you typed it. One backspace takes the change back. This needs autocorrect on and the Vietnamese word list on the device.
The digits that the number row and the keypad show while you type %1$s

You select the digits for %1$s: its own digits, which are %2$s, or 0-9. This applies to this language only. The keys always show the digits that you select. To set where the keyboard also types them, open Layout & size, then Numerals.
Do not show in the language switcher
Keep this language for its suggestions only

%1$s stays on, but the globe key, the spacebar swipe and the language list do not stop at it. Its words continue to show on each keyboard that has it below Also suggest from. Use this when you want a language only for its words, such as English suggestions on a Swedish keyboard, and one keyboard less to switch through.
On the phonetic layout, hello stays hello

With English picked above, the phonetic layout's strip already carries the word exactly as you typed it, in Latin letters, and leans English once the text around it is English.

This goes one step further: a word that reads as English and not as %1$s is written in English when you press space, and shows that way while you type it. Words both languages have follow the language of the words around them, and the word just before counts most: am after I is English, and the same letters on their own are not. A capital I on its own is always the English word. A capital letter anywhere after the first always means the phonetic layout.

When the keyboard picks wrong, press backspace straight after the word to flip it to the other script, or tap the other one on the strip. It remembers, and after two flips it stops asking about that spelling.
Keep the first two words in place
What you typed first, the %1$s word next, then suggestions

Usually the first word on the strip is the word that the space bar will write, so the words move as you type.

With this on, the first two words always stay in the same place. On the left is what you typed, in English letters. Next to it is the %1$s that the phonetic rules make from it, letter for letter. The suggestions come after them. Tap the left word to write in English, or the word next to it to write the exact %1$s reading.

The space bar does not change: it writes the same word as before. That word shows in bold, and in the autocorrect word color if you set one. The strip does not put a word in the middle on this layout, so that the left word is always first.
Type English words as English on Khipro
Separate from Avro\'s. Off, English words wait on the strip

With English picked above, keys that spell an English word, and no Bangla word the list or your dictionary knows, are written in English when you press space: hello stays hello, and ami is still আমি.

Off, the space bar always writes the Bangla the keys spell, and an English word is only ever a chip on the strip, written when you tap it.

Keys typed into the middle of a word are never taken as English, whichever way this is set. Avro has its own switch, so turning one on leaves the other as it was.
prshn/ next to প্রশ্ন on the strip

Khipro keys such as f and / change the letters before them, so the word on the strip does not always show which keys you pressed.

With this on, the second word on the strip is the keys exactly as you pressed them, modifiers included. Tap it to write those keys as they are, in English letters. The space bar does not change: it writes the Bengali word.

With this off, the keys show only when they are all letters and English is mixed in on the layout, for English words that the dictionary does not know.
Which language fills the rest of the strip
Both languages. The language of the word and of the text around it comes first, and the best word of the other language gets the last place
Only %1$s words from the word list and the known spellings
Only English words that start with what you typed
The words desktop Avro shows under the word you type
The rules this version came with, from %1$s. Newer ones are looked for once a day while you type with Khipro. Tap to check now.
Updated rules from %1$s. Tap to check for newer ones.
Rules from %1$s. The last check installed nothing: %2$s. Tap to try again.
Rules from %1$s. This build has no internet, so newer rules come in from a file: Import from a file on this screen takes the set\'s files.
The rules this version came with. This build cannot update them.
Khipro\'s rules are up to date
Go back to the rules this version came with. The daily check leaves them until a newer set is published.
The words only desktop Avro knows, %1$s to download. Tap to download.
The words only desktop Avro knows, %1$s

Desktop Avro shows a short list under the word you type. The list is built the same way here. First comes the known spelling for what you typed, if there is one. Next come the %1$s dictionary words that sound like it, and the words made by adding an ending to one of them, such as বন্ধু + দের. The words closest to the letter-for-letter reading come first. Last is the letter-for-letter reading itself.

In the suggestion strip: the word that the space bar will write stays first, and the list follows it. Bar above the strip: the whole list goes in a row of its own above the strip, and you can scroll through it. The row stays while the layout is on, so the keyboard does not change height between words.

The space bar writes the same word with all three choices.
The strip shows its usual suggestions
The strip shows the list after the word the space bar will write
A row above the strip shows the whole list, and you can scroll it
Up to three more readings of the word from a small AI model, after the word the space bar writes. %1$s to download, shared by every language

IndicXlit, a model by AI4Bharat, has learned from millions of words how people write %1$s in Latin letters, so it often knows the word when the spelling is loose, such as valobashi or bhalobasi for ভালোবাসি.
Its readings come right after the word the space bar will write. That word never changes, and the model never corrects anything by itself: tap one of its readings to use it. Readings that are in the word list come first. Let it choose the word, below, changes that for spellings the keyboard has no word for.
The model runs on the phone, and nothing you type leaves it. One download covers Bengali, Hindi, Urdu, Assamese, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi, Odia, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam.
The model is a %1$s download, and ONNX Runtime about 33 MB more if it is not here yet.
When the rules spell no known word, the space bar writes the model\'s best reading from the word list

The space bar usually writes what the phonetic rules spell. When that is not a word in the %1$s word list or among your own words, and the known-spellings list has nothing for what you typed, this lets the model\'s best reading that is in the word list go first instead, so a space writes it. The rules\' spelling comes right after it in the strip, one tap away.
On test words the space bar wrote the right word 56%% of the time instead of 25%% in Bengali, and 49%% instead of 41%% in Hindi. The cost: a name or a rare word spelled exactly by the rules, but missing from the word list, can come out as a listed word that looks like it. About one such spelling in six did in Bengali, one in fifteen in Hindi. Words the list knows are left alone.
Neural suggestions turn off on every language that has them. Turning them on again downloads the model again.
Not downloaded, %1$s. Tap to download. Dictation in Latin letters then spells the words the keyboard does not know the way people write them.
Dictation in Latin letters goes back to the spelling rules for the words the keyboard does not know. Tap the row to download the model again.
A small button beside the suggestions turns English words on and off as you type

The button shows on this language\'s phonetic layout and is lit while English words are on. It is for the moment a word keeps coming out in the wrong script: tap it in the middle of the word and the word turns back before you press space.\n\nOff takes the button away and leaves the setting above exactly as you set it, so English words simply stay on. Shared by every language with a phonetic layout.
Tap twice for আ or এ
On Probhat, Jatiya and BSTI, after a vowel: one tap gives য়া or য়ে, a second tap gives আ or এ

After a vowel, the আ-কার and এ-কার keys write য়া and য়ে, as in কায়া and দিয়ে, because a bare া or ে cannot follow a vowel. With this on, pressing the key again straight away turns য়া into আ and য়ে into এ. Holding either key offers আ or এ whether this is on or not. Off by default, because a quick double press then types the glide twice.
An ANSI button on the Bengali layouts writes Bijoy-style text, so আ comes out as Av

ANSI is how Bengali was written before Unicode, in Bijoy and in fonts like SutonnyMJ: each Bengali letter is stored as a Latin character, and the font draws it as Bengali. Some design software and older documents still need it.

With this on, every Bengali layout gets an ANSI button beside the suggestions. Tap it and what you type goes into the text box as ANSI, so আমার সোনার বাংলা becomes Avgvi †mvbvi evsjv. Tap it again for Unicode.

The word you are typing shows as Unicode until you finish it. ANSI text only reads as Bengali in an ANSI font, so keep the button off everywhere else.
Pick the one your ANSI font is made for

The ANSI fonts do not all put the letters in the same places, so there are three versions. Version 2 is the common one, used by SutonnyMJ and most Bijoy fonts. If the text comes out as the wrong letters in your font, try another version.
A Zawgyi button on the Burmese layouts writes text for Zawgyi fonts

Zawgyi is the font encoding most Burmese text was written in before Unicode, and many phones, apps and friends still use it. It uses the same characters as Unicode but puts them in a different order, so text written for one reads as broken letters in the other.
With this on, every Burmese layout gets a Zawgyi button beside the suggestions. Tap it and what you type goes into the text box as Zawgyi. Tap it again for Unicode. Suggestions, autocorrect and the word list keep working in Unicode while you type.
The word you are typing shows as Unicode until you finish it. When the text box already holds Zawgyi, the keyboard offers to write Zawgyi there even with the button off.
Draw the Burmese keys in Noto Sans Myanmar, for a phone whose own font is Zawgyi

A phone set up for Zawgyi has a Zawgyi font in place of its Myanmar font, and that font shows Unicode letters in the wrong order. The keyboard\'s keys and suggestions are Unicode, so on such a phone they can look broken.
With this on, the keyboard draws Burmese in its own copy of Noto Sans Myanmar, a Unicode font, whatever font the phone uses. The font is downloaded once from WM Keyboard\'s data repository (195 KB) the first time the keys need it. A Myanmar font you picked under Appearance still comes first.
The keyboard offers words from these languages while you type %1$s. Autocorrect never changes them.
%1$s and %2$s now suggest each other\'s words. You can change this on each language\'s page.
Each item works offline after the download. The checkbox turns an item off and keeps the file. Delete removes the file from the device.
Built-in list. A bigger list is available.
For suggestions, autocorrect and glide typing

resources.string: The word pairs for next-word predictions download with it, about %1$s.
The list on your device stays in place until the new one has finished downloading, and is then replaced by it.
Not on this phone. This build has no internet: Get the files on the Language pack row lists it, and Import there takes it.
Words your imported Hunspell dictionary accepts, compound words included, are never autocorrected, and its spellings join the suggestions.
Its word list is switched off. Switch it on under Custom dictionaries to check words with it.
This build of the app has no Hunspell library. Suggestions come from the word list alone.
Hunspell is an extra part of the keyboard, about 4 MB with the GiellaLT speller engine it comes with. Download it to check words and compound words against your imported dictionary.
Hunspell is a separate download of about 4 MB.
A finite-state speller from GiellaLT that knows every inflected and compound form. %1$s download, %2$s on the phone, %3$s.
GiellaLT builds a speller for this language. Import its .bhfst, or the .pkt.tar.zst from a GiellaLT release, to check words with it.
Version %1$s, %2$s. Words it accepts are never autocorrected, and its spellings join the suggestions.
Imported, %1$s. Words it accepts are never autocorrected, and its spellings join the suggestions.
The speller did not download or unpack. Check the connection and the free storage.
This build of the app has no spelling library. Suggestions come from the word lists alone.
That file is not a speller. Pick a .bhfst, a .zhfst or a GiellaLT .pkt.tar.zst.
That speller would not open. It may be damaged or made for a newer divvunspell.
Spell checking is an extra part of the keyboard, about 4 MB. Download it to use a GiellaLT speller.
Finnish spell checking that knows compound words and every inflection, used in place of a Hunspell dictionary. %1$s download, %2$s on the phone, %3$s.
Import a Voikko dictionary, a zip with a 5/mor-standard folder in it, to check words with it.
Dictionary %1$s, %2$s. Words Voikko accepts are never autocorrected, and its spellings join the suggestions.
Imported, %1$s. Words Voikko accepts are never autocorrected, and its spellings join the suggestions.
The dictionary did not download. Check the connection and the free storage.
This build of the app has no Voikko library. Suggestions come from the word lists and any imported Hunspell dictionary.
That file is not a Voikko dictionary. Pick a zip with a 5/mor-standard folder in it.
That dictionary would not load. It may be damaged or made for a newer Voikko.
Spell checking is an extra part of the keyboard, about 4.5 MB. Download it to check Finnish with Voikko.
Voikko checks this language instead while its dictionary is on the phone.
Download a bigger conversion dictionary. It holds many more characters and phrases than the built-in set. It works offline after the download.
Read a FlorisBoard language pack (.flex). It can fill the Cangjie and stroke tables above.
The app read %1$s and added %2$d characters.
This pack holds %1$s. This keyboard types Cangjie and stroke, so there is nothing in it to use.
That file is a FlorisBoard theme or keyboard extension, not a language pack. To import a theme, go to Themes.
The app cannot read that file as a FlorisBoard language pack.

The built-in engine converts with the dictionaries above. RIME is the open-source engine behind Weasel, Squirrel and Trime. It reads RIME schemas, learns the words you pick, and can type schemas you import yourself. It needs its own library and schema packs, which it compiles on the phone.
With RIME, the layouts of this language convert through the RIME schema you pick for each. The keys stay the same.
RIME needs its library, about %1$s. The built-in engine types until it is here.
RIME needs its library. The built-in engine types until it is here.
The RIME library did not download.
Download a schema pack below. RIME starts when one is compiled.
RIME starts after you unlock the phone. Until then the built-in engine types.
The schemas changed and need to be compiled again.
A zip with .schema.yaml and .dict.yaml files, such as a schema from GitHub. They are compiled with the packs.
That zip has no RIME schema in it.
Which compiled schema each kind of layout types through. Automatic takes the first downloaded pack that has one.
Removes the compiled schemas, your imported schemas and the words RIME learned from you. Downloaded packs stay and compile again.

The built-in engine converts with the kana dictionary above. Mozc is Google\'s open-source Japanese engine, the one behind Google Japanese Input. It converts whole sentences, learns what you pick, and lets you move the boundaries between the parts of a reading. It needs its own library and dictionary.
With Mozc, every Japanese layout converts through Mozc: romaji, flick, 12-key and kana. The keys stay the same. The arrow keys resize the part of the reading being converted.
Mozc needs its library, about %1$s. The built-in engine types until it is here.
Mozc needs its library. The built-in engine types until it is here.
The Mozc library did not download.
Mozc starts when you pick it above.
Mozc starts after you unlock the phone. Until then the built-in engine types.
Download the Mozc dictionary below. Mozc starts when it is here.
Clears the conversions, predictions and reading boundaries Mozc learned from your picks. The dictionary stays.
The keyboard converts candidates to Traditional (繁體). With the phrase table pack, it converts word by word, so 头发 becomes 頭髮.

The keyboard converts each candidate from Simplified (简体) to Traditional (繁體) before it shows the candidate. Some Simplified characters have more than one Traditional form, and the word decides which one is correct: 发 is 發 in 發展 but 髮 in 頭髮, and 后 is 後 in 後來 but 后 in 皇后. With the phrase table pack downloaded, the keyboard reads whole words, so it writes the correct form. Without the pack, or for a word that is in no table, it converts one character at a time.
A button beside the candidates switches between Simplified and Traditional
Show the reading in the text field
Off, the pinyin you type shows only on the keyboard, before the candidates

On, the pinyin, zhuyin or Jyutping that you type shows underlined in the text field until you pick a candidate. Off, the text field stays as it is, and the keyboard shows what you typed at the start of the candidate strip. Only the candidate you pick goes into the text field, the way fcitx5 works.
The best candidates for everything that you typed go into the text field
The pinyin or zhuyin goes into the text field as letters, the way fcitx5 does it
Nothing goes into the text field

Taiwan and Hong Kong each prefer some character forms of their own. Taiwan also often uses different words for the same thing, for example 計程車 for 出租車. Only Taiwan wording changes the words. The other choices keep the word that you typed.
Characters only, no changes to wording
Character preferences of Taiwan, no changes to wording
Changes words to the Taiwan words: 出租車 to 計程車, 光盤 to 光碟
On this phone. Select Korean text and tap Fix spacing.
About 18 MB. Fix spacing needs this and the model above.
Show the Hanja for the word you are typing on the suggestion strip
Tap one to write it in place of the Hangul. An ending stays in Hangul, so 학교에 can become 學校에. Needs the Hanja dictionary above. To see every choice for a word, turn on the scrolling suggestion strip.
Match merged sounds: n↔l, ng↔∅, gw→g before -o, -ng↔-n, -k↔-t…
かつこう also finds 学校 (がっこう)

On the Flick and Kana JIS layouts, a small kana, a ゛ or a ゜ is an extra key. With this on, a plain kana also matches those forms: か finds が, つ finds っ and づ, は finds ば and ぱ, や finds ゃ. When two words are almost equally common, the one that you typed exactly comes first. A kana that you typed with a mark is not changed, and Romaji typing is not changed.
The space bar types a full-width space [ ]

Japanese and Chinese text is spaced with the ideographic space (U+3000), which is as wide as one character. With this on, the space bar types it instead of the narrow space used between words in other languages. A space pressed while you are still typing a reading picks a candidate as before, and only a press with nothing waiting to convert types a space.
Space highlights the next candidate, and Enter types it

Off, the space bar types the first candidate straight away. On, the first press highlights it and each press after moves to the next one, the way Japanese input methods work. Enter types the highlighted candidate, typing on keeps it and starts a new reading, and backspace goes back to the reading. With a physical keyboard, the arrow keys move the highlight either way, Enter or space types it, and once something is highlighted the keys 1 to 9 pick a candidate and Escape goes back to the reading.
Type only the first letter of a syllable: wm finds 我们, zg finds 中国

A letter that is not a whole syllable stands for every syllable that starts with it, so wm finds 我们 and haod finds 好的. Each letter is one syllable: hd means h… plus d…. A syllable that you type in full is matched exactly and ranks first. The letters z, c and s also cover zh, ch and sh. A Double Pinyin scheme does not use this, because every syllable is exactly two keys there.
After you pick Chinese text, show the words that usually come next

When a conversion is complete and nothing is composing, the strip shows the words that usually follow the text before the cursor. Tap one to type it, and the strip shows what follows that. The words that you write after others come first, then the common word pairs, then the rest of a word that the last character starts (无 gives 聊). This needs the word pairs pack.
rq types the date, sj the time, xq the weekday, v and a number gives Chinese numerals

Type rq for the date, sj for the time and xq for the weekday. These show after the best candidate for the same letters. Type v and then a number, for example v1234.5, to get it as 一千二百三十四点五, as 壹仟贰佰叁拾肆点伍 for amounts, or digit by digit. No pinyin syllable starts with v, so this does not change pinyin.
Match confusable sounds: zh↔z, ch↔c, sh↔s, n↔l, an↔ang, in↔ing…

Pick the sounds you want matched. Every one is on to start with. Switching a pair off makes your spelling of it exact again, which gives you back some precision: the ending pairs are a regional accent and cost you little, while n↔l affects every syllable that starts with either.
Double Pinyin: type each syllable with exactly two keys. It needs the Pinyin dictionary above.
Set your own keys. Copy, paste, import or export the scheme, in the same format as fcitx
This replaces the text in the editor with that scheme\'s keys. Nothing is saved until you press Save.
Saved. The keyboard now types with this scheme.
File read in. Press Save to type with it.
That file could not be read
The file could not be written
No scheme yet. Write one, paste one, or start from a built-in scheme in the menu. While this is empty, you type full Pinyin.
Every initial and final has a key
